name: Nullspace / linear-algebra kernel
short: Every vector a linear map sends to zero.
body: The kernel, or nullspace, of a linear map A is the subspace of inputs x satisfying Ax = 0. It records directions that the map loses.
example: For A = [1  2], every vector t(−2, 1) maps to zero. The kernel is a line, not the zero vector alone.
note: A matrix used as an image filter is also called a kernel, but its nullspace is a different object.

name: Group-homomorphism kernel
short: Group elements sent to the identity.
body: For a group homomorphism φ, the kernel is the preimage of the target group's identity. It is a normal subgroup; quotienting by it removes exactly the distinctions that φ loses.
example: Reduction modulo 3 maps the additive group of integers to ℤ/3ℤ. Its kernel is 3ℤ.
note: Zero is the identity for additive groups. For multiplicative groups, use the identity 1 instead.

name: Ring-homomorphism kernel
short: Ring elements sent to zero; an ideal.
body: The zero fiber of a ring homomorphism is an ideal. In algebraic geometry, such kernels can encode equations imposed by a map of coordinate rings.
example: Evaluation at 2 sends a polynomial p(x) to p(2). Over ℝ[x], its kernel is the ideal generated by x−2.
note: In the category of unital rings, the zero map is generally not a unital morphism. The ideal kernel and the categorical zero-map construction need care.

name: Categorical kernel
short: A universal arrow on which a morphism becomes zero.
body: In a category with zero morphisms, a kernel of f:A→B is an arrow k:K→A that equalizes f and the zero arrow, with the corresponding universal property.
example: For vector spaces, K is the usual nullspace and k includes it into A. Every map g with fg=0 factors uniquely through k.
note: The categorical kernel includes a morphism and a universal property. Not every category has zero arrows or kernels.

name: Congruence / function kernel
short: Pairs of inputs that have the same output.
body: Another convention calls the equivalence relation f(x)=f(y) the kernel of f. For a homomorphism of universal algebras, this relation is compatible with the algebra's operations: a congruence.
example: For f(n)=n mod 3, the relation groups integers into three equivalence classes. It contains every pair differing by a multiple of 3.
note: This kernel is a set of pairs, not just the zero equivalence class 3ℤ.

name: Differential-operator kernel
body: The nullspace idea also applies to spaces of functions. The kernel of a differential operator consists of solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, in a specified function space and with any imposed boundary conditions.
example: On an interval, the kernel of d/dx consists of constant functions. The kernel of the Laplacian consists of harmonic functions.
note: A Green kernel represents a solution operator; it is not the nullspace of the differential operator. Domains and boundary conditions matter.

sources.title: Laplace equation and the kernel of a differential operator

name: Isogeny kernel
short: Points mapped to the identity of another elliptic curve.
body: An isogeny is a suitable group-preserving algebraic map between elliptic curves. Its point kernel over an algebraic closure is finite. For separable isogenies, the finite subgroup determines the quotient isogeny up to isomorphism.
example: Over characteristic zero, the doubling map [2] has the identity and three nonzero 2-torsion points in its kernel.
note: In positive characteristic, inseparability makes the distinction between geometric points and the kernel group scheme important.

name: Kernel pair
short: The pullback that records inputs identified by a map.
body: Where the relevant pullback exists, the kernel pair of f:A→B is A×ᵦA with its two projections to A. In sets it consists of pairs with equal f-images.
example: The kernel pair of reduction modulo 3 records two integers whenever their residues agree.
note: A kernel pair need not require a zero object. It generalizes the relation kernel, rather than the zero fiber alone.

name: Module / Lie-algebra kernel
short: A submodule or ideal consisting of zero-mapped elements.
body: A module homomorphism's zero fiber is a submodule. A Lie-algebra homomorphism's zero fiber is a Lie ideal. These are algebraic versions of the same map-to-zero idea.
example: The homomorphism ℤ → ℤ/4ℤ has kernel 4ℤ, viewed as a ℤ-submodule of ℤ.
note: Different ambient algebraic structures impose different closure properties on the kernel.

sources.title: Universal property of kernels and cokernels

name: Parity-check kernel
short: The nullspace describing all valid codewords.
body: A linear code can be specified as the vectors annihilated by a parity-check matrix H over a finite field.
example: Over 𝔽₂, H=[1 1 1] defines {000, 011, 101, 110}: exactly the binary triples with even parity.
note: Arithmetic is in the stated finite field, not ordinary real arithmetic. This is a use of the linear-algebra kernel.
